bricks.title: Gross Anatomy and Histology of the Oral Region

items.why: Lip sphincter; oral competence; labial sounds

questions.q: The orbicularis oris primarily acts as a:
questions.explain: The orbicularis oris is the sphincter of the mouth, enabling lip closure and articulation of labial sounds (/p/, /b/, /m/).

questions.q: After a stroke, a patient drools and leaks liquid from the mouth when drinking. Loss of which muscle's function best explains this?
questions.explain: The orbicularis oris provides oral competence (a complete lip seal); its loss, as after a CVA, causes drooling and leakage of food or liquid.

items.excerpt: The orbicularis oris … functions as a sphincter of the mouth, enabling lip closure and articulation of labial sounds

items.why: Cheek muscle; keeps food between teeth; pierced by parotid duct

questions.q: What is the main role of the buccinator during chewing?
questions.explain: The buccinator works with the tongue to keep food between the occlusal surfaces of the teeth, preventing food from collecting in the vestibule.

questions.q: Which duct crosses the buccinator muscle to open into the mouth?
questions.explain: The parotid (Stensen's) duct crosses the buccinator and opens into the oral vestibule opposite the maxillary second molar.

items.excerpt: The buccinator works with the tongue to keep food between the occlusal surfaces of the teeth during mastication

items.why: Stensen's duct opens in vestibule opposite maxillary 2nd molar

questions.q: Where does the parotid duct open?
questions.explain: The parotid (Stensen's) duct opens into the oral vestibule opposite the maxillary second molar, a landmark for assessing gland function or obstruction.

questions.q: The parotid duct empties into which compartment of the mouth?
questions.explain: The oral vestibule lies between the lips/cheeks and the teeth/gums; the parotid duct opens into it opposite the maxillary second molar.

items.excerpt: The parotid duct (Stensen's duct) … crosses the buccinator muscle and opens into the oral vestibule opposite the maxillary second molar.

items.why: Protrudes tongue; CN XII

questions.q: What is the main action of the genioglossus?
questions.explain: Genioglossus protrudes the tongue; hyoglossus depresses, styloglossus retracts and elevates, and palatoglossus elevates the posterior tongue.

questions.q: Which nerve supplies the genioglossus?
questions.explain: All tongue muscles are innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) except the palatoglossus, which is supplied by the vagus (CN X).

items.excerpt: The tongue will deviate toward the side of the CN XII lesion on protrusion because the intact genioglossus muscle pulls the tongue forward

items.why: Depresses tongue

questions.q: What is the action of the hyoglossus?
questions.explain: The hyoglossus depresses the tongue; it is an extrinsic muscle innervated by CN XII.

items.excerpt: Hyoglossus - depresses the tongue

items.why: Retracts and elevates tongue

questions.q: What is the action of the styloglossus?
questions.explain: The styloglossus retracts and elevates the tongue; intrinsic muscles (not attached to bone) are the ones that only change its shape.

items.excerpt: Styloglossus - retracts and elevates the tongue

items.why: Elevates posterior tongue; CN X; anterior pillar of fauces

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the palatoglossus?
questions.explain: The palatoglossus is the one tongue muscle not supplied by CN XII; it is innervated by the vagus nerve (CN X).

questions.q: The palatoglossal fold forms which part of the fauces?
questions.explain: The fauces are bounded by the palatoglossal folds (anterior pillars) and palatopharyngeal folds (posterior pillars), with the palatine tonsils between them.

items.excerpt: Palatoglossus muscle … elevates the posterior tongue and is innervated by CN X

items.why: Motor to tongue; lesion -> deviation toward lesion

questions.q: A patient with a right hypoglossal nerve lesion protrudes the tongue. Which way does it deviate?
questions.explain: The tongue deviates toward the side of the CN XII lesion because the intact contralateral genioglossus pushes it forward and across unopposed.

questions.q: Which tongue muscle is NOT innervated by the hypoglossal nerve?
questions.explain: All tongue muscles are supplied by CN XII except the palatoglossus, which is innervated by CN X.

items.excerpt: All tongue muscles are innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), except the palatoglossus, which is innervated by the vagus nerve (CN X).

items.why: General sensation anterior 2/3 tongue (V3); in sublingual space

questions.q: General sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the:
questions.explain: The lingual nerve (branch of CN V3) carries general sensation from the anterior two-thirds; the chorda tympani carries taste from the same region.

questions.q: The lingual nerve runs in which space of the floor of the mouth?
questions.explain: Superior to the mylohyoid lies the sublingual space, which contains the sublingual glands, lingual nerve, and submandibular duct.

items.excerpt: General sensation: Lingual nerve (branch of CN V₃)

items.why: Palatine processes of maxillae + horizontal plates of palatine bones

questions.q: The hard palate is formed by the palatine processes of the maxillae and the:
choices: Pterygoid plates of the sphenoid bone
Horizontal plates of the palatine bones
questions.explain: The hard palate is formed by the palatine processes of the maxillae and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones, providing a rigid surface for tongue-mediated food manipulation.

items.excerpt: The hard palate is a bony structure formed by the palatine processes of the maxillae, and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones

items.why: Elevates to close nasopharynx; hypernasal speech / nasal regurgitation

questions.q: During swallowing, the soft palate elevates to:
questions.explain: The soft palate elevates against the posterior pharyngeal wall to close off the nasopharynx, preventing food from entering the nasal cavity.

questions.q: Inadequate elevation of the soft palate most directly causes:
questions.explain: Inadequate soft palate elevation produces hypernasal speech, and incomplete closure allows nasal regurgitation during swallowing.

items.excerpt: During swallowing, the soft palate elevates to close off the nasopharynx by contacting the posterior pharyngeal wall, preventing food from entering the nasal cavity.

items.why: 'Say ahh' tests CN X via uvula/soft palate

questions.q: Asking a patient to say "ahh" to check uvula position tests which nerve?
questions.explain: Saying "ahh" shows soft palate elevation and uvula position; uvula deviation or poor elevation indicates vagus nerve (CN X) dysfunction.

items.excerpt: Its free posterior margin contains the uvula … a midline projection visible during oral examination.

items.why: Lymphoid tissue between palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal folds

questions.q: The palatine tonsils lie in the tonsillar fossa between which folds?
questions.explain: The palatine tonsils sit between the palatoglossal (anterior) and palatopharyngeal (posterior) folds, at the junction of the oral cavity and oropharynx.

items.excerpt: The palatine tonsils are lymphoid tissue involved in immune surveillance and are commonly enlarged or infected in children.

items.why: Floor of mouth; separates sublingual from submandibular space (Ludwig's)

questions.q: In Ludwig's angina, infection spreads from the floor of the mouth into the neck across which muscle?
questions.explain: The mylohyoid forms the floor of the mouth, separating the sublingual space above from the submandibular space below; infection crossing it reaches the neck.

questions.q: Which space lies immediately inferior to the mylohyoid?
questions.explain: Inferior to the mylohyoid lies the submandibular space, which communicates with deeper cervical spaces.

items.excerpt: The floor of the mouth is primarily formed by the mylohyoid muscle … a partition between the oral cavity and the neck.

items.why: Opens at sublingual caruncle beside frenulum

questions.q: Where does the submandibular duct open into the mouth?
questions.explain: The submandibular ducts run anteriorly along the floor of the mouth and open at the sublingual papillae (caruncles) on either side of the lingual frenulum.

items.excerpt: The bilateral submandibular ducts run anteriorly along the floor of the mouth and open at small elevations called the sublingual papillae (caruncle)

items.why: Taste anterior 2/3 via chorda tympani; lip movement

questions.q: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue travels in which nerve?
questions.explain: Taste from the anterior two-thirds is carried by the chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII); general sensation travels in the lingual nerve.

questions.q: Assessing lip movement and symmetry during an oral exam tests which cranial nerve?
questions.explain: In the oral exam, CN VII is assessed by lip movement and symmetry; CN V by mucosal sensation, CN X by palate elevation, and CN XII by tongue protrusion.

items.excerpt: Facial nerve (CN VII): Lip movement and symmetry

items.why: General sensation of oral mucosa and anterior tongue

questions.q: General sensation of the oral mucosa is assessed as a test of which cranial nerve?
questions.explain: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) provides general sensation to the oral mucosa and, via the lingual branch of V3, the anterior tongue.

items.excerpt: Trigeminal nerve (CN V): general sensation of oral mucosa and anterior tongue

items.why: Say 'ahh' tests CN X; motor to palatoglossus
items.excerpt: During examination, asking a patient to say "ahh" allows visualization of soft palate elevation and assessment of vagus nerve (CN X) function.

items.why: Masseter/temporalis/medial pterygoid elevate; lateral pterygoid protrudes

questions.q: Which muscle of mastication assists protrusion and side-to-side grinding rather than elevating the mandible?
questions.explain: Masseter, temporalis, and medial pterygoid elevate the mandible; the lateral pterygoid assists with protrusion and lateral grinding movements.

items.excerpt: masseter, temporalis, and medial pterygoid muscles elevate the mandible; lateral pterygoid assists with protrusion and lateral movements for grinding

items.why: Purely serous; amylase

questions.q: The secretion of the parotid gland is best described as:
questions.explain: The parotid gland consists entirely of serous acini producing amylase, which breaks down complex carbohydrates.

items.excerpt: The parotid gland consists entirely of serous acini with cells producing amylase and other proteins for storage in secretory granules.

items.why: Mixed gland; 2/3 of saliva

questions.q: Which gland produces about two-thirds of all saliva?
questions.explain: The submandibular gland, a mixed sero-mucous gland, produces about two-thirds of all saliva.

items.excerpt: The submandibular gland produces 2/3 of all saliva. It is a mixed sero-mucous gland

items.why: In sublingual space with lingual n. and submandibular duct

questions.q: Along with the sublingual glands, the sublingual space contains:
questions.explain: Superior to the mylohyoid, the sublingual space contains the sublingual glands, lingual nerve, and submandibular duct.

items.excerpt: The sublingual gland predominantly consists of mucous acini with mucus as their main product; few serous acini are present

groups.title: Floor of the Mouth and Sublingual Region

items.why: Gives three unpaired anterior gut branches

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the three unpaired anterior branches of the abdominal aorta that supply the GI tract?
questions.explain: The GI tract is supplied by three unpaired anterior aortic branches: the celiac trunk, SMA, and IMA. The renal arteries are paired lateral branches.

items.excerpt: The gastrointestinal (GI) tract is supplied by three unpaired anterior branches of the abdominal aorta.

items.why: Foregut artery: left gastric, splenic, common hepatic

questions.q: What are the three branches of the celiac trunk?
questions.explain: The celiac trunk gives rise to the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries, which supply foregut structures.

questions.q: Which organ receives its blood supply from the celiac trunk?
questions.explain: The celiac trunk supplies foregut derivatives (abdominal esophagus, stomach, proximal duodenum); the cecum and jejunum are SMA and the descending colon is IMA.

items.excerpt: The foregut gives rise to the abdominal esophagus, stomach, and proximal duodenum. These structures are supplied by branches of the celiac trunk.

items.why: Gives left gastroepiploic and short gastrics

questions.q: Which celiac branch gives rise to the short gastric and left gastroepiploic arteries?
questions.explain: The splenic artery gives the short gastric arteries (fundus) and the left gastroepiploic artery (greater curvature).

items.excerpt: The celiac trunk gives rise to three primary branches: the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries

items.why: Abdominal esophagus + lesser curvature

questions.q: Which artery supplies the abdominal portion of the esophagus?
questions.explain: Only the abdominal esophagus is supplied by the left gastric artery, a celiac branch, which is why it is classed as foregut.

questions.q: The left gastric artery arises directly from the:
questions.explain: The left gastric is one of the three primary celiac branches and runs along the lesser curvature to anastomose with the right gastric.

items.excerpt: Only the abdominal esophagus is supplied by the left gastric artery (a branch of the celiac trunk) and is therefore considered part of the foregut.

items.why: Only abdominal part is foregut (left gastric a.)
items.excerpt: The esophagus is divided into cervical, thoracic, and abdominal portions, each with a distinct blood supply.

items.why: Celiac branches anastomose along both curvatures
items.excerpt: The stomach is supplied by branches of the celiac trunk that form arterial anastomoses along its curvatures.

items.why: Lesser curvature; from proper hepatic

questions.q: The right gastric artery most directly arises from the:
questions.explain: On the lesser curvature, the right gastric (from the proper hepatic) anastomoses with the left gastric (from the celiac trunk).

items.excerpt: Lesser curvature → right gastric artery (from the proper hepatic artery) and left gastric artery (from the celiac trunk)

items.why: Gives right gastric
items.excerpt: right gastric artery (from the proper hepatic artery)

items.why: Greater curvature (from GDA)

questions.q: The right gastroepiploic artery supplies which part of the stomach?
questions.explain: The greater curvature is supplied by the right gastroepiploic (from the GDA) and left gastroepiploic (from the splenic) arteries.

items.excerpt: right gastroepiploic artery (aka right gastroomental) from the gastroduodenal artery

items.why: Greater curvature (from splenic)

questions.q: Along the greater curvature, the left gastroepiploic artery anastomoses with the:
questions.explain: The left (from the splenic) and right (from the GDA) gastroepiploic arteries form the greater-curvature anastomosis.

items.excerpt: left gastroepiploic artery (aka left gastroomental) from the splenic artery

items.why: Supply fundus (from splenic)

questions.q: The short gastric arteries supply which region of the stomach?
questions.explain: The short gastric arteries, branches of the splenic artery, supply the fundus.

items.excerpt: Fundus → short gastric arteries (from the splenic artery)

items.why: Celiac branch -> GDA + proper hepatic

questions.q: The common hepatic artery branches into which two arteries?
questions.explain: The common hepatic artery gives the proper hepatic artery and the gastroduodenal artery, which in turn supplies the proximal duodenum and greater curvature.

items.excerpt: the gastroduodenal artery, a branch of the common hepatic artery

items.why: Gives right gastroepiploic + superior pancreaticoduodenals

questions.q: Which artery gives rise to the right gastroepiploic artery?
questions.explain: The right gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) artery comes from the gastroduodenal artery and runs along the greater curvature.

items.excerpt: The proximal duodenum is supplied by the supraduodenal and superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries … which arise from the gastroduodenal artery

items.why: Proximal duodenum; from GDA

questions.q: The anterior and posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries arise from the:
questions.explain: The proximal duodenum is supplied by the supraduodenal and superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries from the gastroduodenal artery.

items.excerpt: superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries (anterior & posterior) which arise from the gastroduodenal artery

items.why: Midgut artery; emboli lodge here; whole-midgut necrosis

questions.q: Cardiac emboli most commonly lodge in which aortic branch?
questions.explain: Emboli favor the SMA because of its large diameter, high flow, and shallow takeoff angle from the aorta.

questions.q: A proximal SMA embolus threatens which bowel segments?
questions.explain: Proximal SMA occlusion can kill the entire midgut: jejunum, ileum, and proximal colon, which is often unsurvivable.

items.excerpt: cardioembolic emboli most commonly lodge in the SMA because of its large diameter, high volume blood flow, and shallow takeoff angle from the aorta.

items.why: Distal duodenum; from SMA

questions.q: The inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery, supplying the distal duodenum, arises from the:
questions.explain: The distal duodenum (beyond the major papilla) is midgut, supplied by the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery and jejunal branches of the SMA.

items.excerpt: Distal duodenum is supplied by the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (anterior & posterior) and proximal jejunal branches of the SMA.

items.why: Jejunum: longer vasa recta, fewer arcades than ileum
items.excerpt: Note that the jejunum has greater vascular perfusion, with longer vasa recta and fewer arterial arcades than the ileum

items.why: SMA branch to cecum; gives appendicular a.

questions.q: The ileocolic artery is a branch of the:
questions.explain: The proximal colon is supplied by the ileocolic, right colic, and middle colic branches of the SMA.

items.excerpt: Proximal colon (cecum, ascending colon, proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon) is supplied by the ileocolic, right colic, and middle colic branches of the SMA.

items.why: Ascending colon (SMA)

questions.q: Which artery supplies the ascending colon?
questions.explain: The ascending colon is midgut, supplied by the right colic (and ileocolic) branches of the SMA.

items.excerpt: Proximal colon … is supplied by the ileocolic, right colic, and middle colic branches of the SMA.

items.why: Proximal 2/3 transverse colon (SMA)

questions.q: The middle colic artery supplies which part of the colon?
questions.explain: The middle colic branch of the SMA supplies the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon, where the midgut ends.

items.excerpt: proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon) is supplied by the ileocolic, right colic, and middle colic branches of the SMA.

items.why: Terminal branch of ileocolic

questions.q: The appendicular artery is a terminal branch of the:
questions.explain: The appendix gets its blood supply primarily from the appendicular artery, a terminal branch of the ileocolic artery.

items.excerpt: The appendix gets its blood supply primarily from the appendicular artery, a terminal branch of the ilecolic artery

items.why: Hindgut artery

questions.q: Which structure is supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery?
questions.explain: The IMA supplies the hindgut: distal third of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, and upper rectum.

items.excerpt: The hindgut gives rise to the distal one-third of the transverse colon … These structures are supplied by branches of the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA)

items.why: IMA branch to distal colon

questions.q: Which artery is an IMA branch supplying the distal colon?
questions.explain: The distal colon is supplied by the left colic and sigmoid arteries, branches of the IMA.

items.excerpt: Distal colon → left colic and sigmoid arteries

items.why: IMA branch; rectosigmoid watershed

questions.q: The rectosigmoid junction is prone to ischemia because it lies at the junction of:
questions.explain: The rectosigmoid junction is a watershed between the IMA (sigmoid/superior rectal) and the rectal arterial supply.

items.excerpt: Rectosigmoid junction → junction of IMA and rectal arterial supply

items.why: Upper rectum; IMA branch

questions.q: The superior rectal artery, supplying the upper rectum, is a branch of the:
questions.explain: The superior rectal artery is the IMA's supply to the upper rectum; the middle and inferior rectal arteries come from the internal iliac and internal pudendal.

items.excerpt: Upper rectum → superior rectal artery

items.why: Splenic flexure = SMA/IMA watershed

questions.q: Which part of the colon is a watershed zone between SMA and IMA territories?
questions.explain: The splenic flexure lies at the junction of the SMA and IMA territories and, with limited collaterals, is vulnerable to ischemic colitis.

items.excerpt: Splenic flexure → junction of SMA and IMA territories

items.why: Formed by SMV + splenic v.; varices via left gastric

questions.q: The hepatic portal vein is formed by the union of the:
questions.explain: The portal vein is formed by the confluence of the splenic vein (often receiving the IMV) and the superior mesenteric vein.

questions.q: In portal hypertension, esophageal varices develop because pressure is transmitted through the:
questions.explain: Raised portal pressure passes to the left gastric vein and its esophageal branches, dilating submucosal veins of the distal esophagus.

items.excerpt: The portal vein is primarily formed by the confluence of the splenic vein (often receiving the inferior mesenteric vein) and the superior mesenteric vein

items.why: Receives left gastroepiploic, short gastrics, IMV

questions.q: The left gastroepiploic and short gastric veins drain into the:
questions.explain: Left gastroepiploic and short gastric veins drain into the splenic vein; right and left gastric veins drain directly into the portal vein.

items.excerpt: Left gastroepiploic and short gastric veins → drain into the splenic vein

items.why: Small bowel + proximal colon; right gastroepiploic v.

questions.q: The right gastroepiploic vein drains into the:
questions.explain: The right gastroepiploic vein drains into the SMV, which also drains the small intestine and proximal colon.

items.excerpt: Venous blood from the small intestine drains into the superior mesenteric vein (SMV), which contributes to formation of the portal vein.

items.why: Distal colon; joins splenic v.

questions.q: The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into the:
questions.explain: The distal colon drains into the IMV, which typically joins the splenic vein before the splenic vein and SMV form the portal vein.

items.excerpt: the distal colon drains into the inferior mesenteric vein (IMV), which typically joins the splenic vein.

items.why: Proximal colon -> SMA/SMV; distal colon -> IMA/IMV
items.excerpt: Venous drainage of the colon reflects its arterial supply. The proximal colon drains into the superior mesenteric vein (SMV)

items.why: Systemic return after liver

questions.q: After passing through the liver, portal blood enters the systemic circulation via the:
questions.explain: The portal system lets the liver process absorbed nutrients before blood enters systemic circulation via the IVC.

items.excerpt: allowing the liver to process absorbed nutrients before the blood enters systemic circulation via the inferior vena cava (IVC).

items.why: Recanalized in portal HTN -> caput medusae

questions.q: Caput medusae in portal hypertension results from recanalization of the:
questions.explain: Elevated portal pressure recanalizes the round ligament, reopening the umbilical vein so blood flows into superficial abdominal wall veins.

items.excerpt: Caput medusae - elevated portal pressures recanalize the round ligament, reopening the umbilical vein and allowing blood to flow into the superficial abdominal wall veins.

items.why: Parasympathetic to foregut + midgut

questions.q: Vagal parasympathetic supply to the GI tract extends as far as the:
questions.explain: The vagus supplies the foregut and midgut, as far as the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon; the hindgut gets pelvic splanchnics.

items.excerpt: The vagus nerve arises from the brainstem and supplies the GI tract as far as the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon (foregut & midgut).

items.why: Anterior = mainly left vagus; posterior = mainly right

questions.q: The anterior vagal trunk is formed mainly from the:
questions.explain: Passing through the diaphragm, the vagus splits into the anterior trunk (mainly left vagus) and posterior trunk (mainly right vagus).

items.excerpt: it splits into the anterior vagal trunk (primarily from the left vagus nerve) and posterior vagal trunks (primarily from the right vagus nerve)

items.why: Parasympathetic S2-S4 to hindgut

questions.q: The pelvic splanchnic nerves carry which fibers?
questions.explain: Pelvic splanchnics are the only parasympathetic splanchnics ("two Ps"), carrying S2–S4 outflow to the hindgut.

items.excerpt: Hindgut → innervated by the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4)

items.why: Sympathetic to foregut/midgut; foregut pain epigastric

questions.q: Sympathetic supply to the foregut and midgut is carried by the:
questions.explain: Thoracic splanchnic nerves carry sympathetics to the foregut and midgut; lumbar splanchnics supply the hindgut.

questions.q: Visceral pain from the stomach (a foregut organ) is typically referred to the:
questions.explain: Foregut afferents enter at T5–T9, so foregut pain is referred to the epigastric region.

items.excerpt: sympathetic innervation of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract decreases motility, secretion, and blood flow. These fibers are carried primarily by thoracic and lumbar splanchnic nerves

items.why: Sympathetic to hindgut; hindgut pain suprapubic

questions.q: Sympathetic innervation of the hindgut is carried by the:
questions.explain: Hindgut sympathetics travel in the lumbar splanchnic nerves; pain afferents follow them to T12–L2, giving suprapubic referred pain.

items.excerpt: These fibers travel through thoracic and lumbar splanchnic nerves to reach preaortic (prevertebral) ganglia located near the major branches of the abdominal aorta.

items.why: Preganglionic sympathetic synapse; celiac block

questions.q: Intractable pain from unresectable pancreatic cancer can be relieved by blocking the:
questions.explain: Celiac plexus block (local anesthetic) or neurolysis (alcohol) interrupts visceral foregut pain transmission.

questions.q: Which fibers synapse in the celiac ganglia?
questions.explain: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers from the splanchnic nerves synapse in preaortic ganglia such as the celiac; postganglionic fibers then follow the arteries.

items.excerpt: Intractable visceral foregut pain, such as that caused by unresectable pancreatic cancer, can be treated with celiac plexus block or neurolysis

items.why: Appendicitis: periumbilical (T10) then RLQ

questions.q: Early appendicitis pain is typically felt in which region?
questions.explain: The appendix is midgut, so early visceral pain is referred to the T10 periumbilical region before localizing to the right lower quadrant.

questions.q: Appendicitis pain shifts to the right lower quadrant because inflammation reaches the:
questions.explain: Once inflammation involves the somatically innervated parietal peritoneum, pain becomes sharply localized to the RLQ.

items.excerpt: Pain in the T10 dermatome (periumbilical region) may be an early sign of appendicitis.

Referred Pain from the GI Tract

items.why: Double peritoneal layer to posterior wall

questions.q: A mesentery is best defined as a double layer of peritoneum that connects:
choices: The stomach to another abdominal organ
An organ to the posterior abdominal wall
One organ directly to another organ
The liver to the anterior abdominal wall
questions.explain: A mesentery connects an organ to the posterior abdominal wall and conducts vessels, nerves, and lymphatics; omenta attach the stomach, and ligaments link organ to organ or wall.

items.excerpt: A mesentery is a double layer of visceral peritoneum that connects an organ to the posterior abdominal wall

items.why: Greater curvature -> transverse colon; walls off infection

questions.q: The greater omentum descends from the greater curvature of the stomach and then ascends to attach to the:
questions.explain: The greater omentum hangs like an apron from the greater curvature and proximal duodenum, folds back, and attaches to the transverse colon.

questions.q: How does the greater omentum help limit the spread of intra-abdominal infection?
choices: It drains pus into the lesser sac
questions.explain: The greater omentum can adhere to inflamed areas, helping wall off and limit the spread of infection.

items.excerpt: The greater omentum extends from the greater curvature of the stomach … ascends to attach to the transverse colon

items.why: Liver to lesser curvature; anterior wall of epiploic foramen

questions.q: The lesser omentum forms the anterior boundary of the:
questions.explain: The lesser omentum forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen, which connects the greater and lesser sacs.

questions.q: The lesser omentum is made up of which two ligaments?
questions.explain: The lesser omentum consists of the hepatogastric (liver to stomach) and hepatoduodenal (liver to duodenum) ligaments.

items.excerpt: The lesser omentum also forms the anterior boundary of an opening known as the omental or epiploic foramen.

items.why: Liver -> lesser curvature; no portal triad

questions.q: The hepatogastric ligament connects the liver to the:
questions.explain: The hepatogastric ligament runs from the liver to the lesser curvature; unlike the hepatoduodenal ligament, it does not carry the portal triad.

items.excerpt: The hepatogastric ligament … connects the liver to the lesser curvature of the stomach and does not contain the portal triad.

items.why: Contains portal triad

questions.q: Which structures run within the hepatoduodenal ligament?
choices: Portal vein, hepatic artery, bile duct
questions.explain: The hepatoduodenal ligament, part of the lesser omentum, contains the portal triad: portal vein, proper hepatic artery, and common bile duct.

items.excerpt: The hepatoduodenal ligament is the clinically important part, as it contains the portal triad: proper hepatic artery, portal vein, and common bile duct.

items.why: Liver to anterior wall; ventral mesentery remnant

questions.q: The falciform ligament anchors the liver to the:
questions.explain: The falciform ligament anchors the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and is a remnant of the embryonic ventral mesentery.

items.excerpt: Falciform ligament: Anchors the liver to the anterior abdominal wall. It is a remnant of the embryonic ventral mesentery.

items.why: Fetal umbilical vein remnant in falciform

questions.q: The ligamentum teres is the remnant of the fetal:
questions.explain: The ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver) is the remnant of the fetal umbilical vein, lying within the falciform ligament.

items.excerpt: Ligamentum teres: Remnant of the fetal umbilical vein within the falciform ligament.

items.why: Liver to diaphragm; bounds bare area

questions.q: The coronary ligament helps define which feature of the liver?
questions.explain: The coronary ligament extends between the diaphragm and liver and outlines the bare area of the liver.

items.excerpt: Coronary ligament: Extends between the diaphragm and the liver and helps define the bare area of the liver.

items.why: Male pouch: rectum-bladder

questions.q: Where is the rectovesical pouch located?
questions.explain: In males the single peritoneal pouch, the rectovesical pouch, lies between the rectum and urinary bladder.

items.excerpt: In males, there is a single pouch, the rectovesical pouch, located between the rectum and the urinary bladder.

items.why: Female pouch: bladder-uterus

questions.q: In females, which pouch lies between the urinary bladder and the uterus?
questions.explain: The vesicouterine pouch lies between the bladder and uterus; the rectouterine pouch lies between the uterus and rectum.

items.excerpt: Vesicouterine pouch: Located between the urinary bladder and the uterus

items.why: Lowest point of female peritoneal cavity

questions.q: Which space is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in a female and a common site for fluid to collect?
questions.explain: The rectouterine pouch (of Douglas), between the uterus and rectum, is the most dependent point of the female peritoneal cavity.

items.excerpt: Rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas): Located between the uterus and the rectum - It is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in females

items.why: Retroperitoneal: ruptured AAA tamponade

questions.q: Why can a patient survive for hours after an abdominal aortic aneurysm ruptures?
choices: Blood drains into the lesser sac
The greater omentum seals the tear
questions.explain: The aorta is retroperitoneal; its closed fascial compartments can temporarily contain hemorrhage, whereas free rupture into the peritoneal cavity is rapidly fatal.

items.excerpt: A ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm that bleeds into the retroperitoneum can sometimes remain contained long enough for the patient to present to the hospital

items.why: Retroperitoneal (SAID PUCKER)
items.excerpt: Major retroperitoneal structures include the suprarenal glands, aorta, inferior vena cava, portions of the duodenum and pancreas

items.why: Secondarily retroperitoneal (except tail)
items.excerpt: Examples of secondarily retroperitoneal structures include the pancreas, duodenum, and the ascending and descending colon.

items.why: Begins at C6; ends at GEJ

questions.q: At which vertebral level does the esophagus begin?
questions.explain: The esophagus begins at the level of C6 and ends at the gastroesophageal junction.

items.excerpt: The esophagus is a muscular tube that transports a bolus of food from the pharynx to the stomach by peristalsis.

items.why: UES; skeletal muscle; vagal relaxation

questions.q: What type of muscle forms the cricopharyngeus (upper esophageal sphincter)?
questions.explain: The UES is formed by the cricopharyngeus, which is skeletal muscle; the LES is a thickening of smooth muscle.

questions.q: During swallowing, the cricopharyngeus relaxes because of:
questions.explain: The UES is tonically contracted at rest; during swallowing, vagal-mediated inhibition relaxes it so the bolus can enter the esophagus.

items.excerpt: The cricopharyngeus muscle, composed of skeletal muscle, forms the UES … During swallowing, vagal-mediated inhibition causes it to relax

items.why: Thickened inner circular smooth muscle; low tone -> GERD

questions.q: The lower esophageal sphincter is formed by a thickening of the:
questions.explain: The LES is a specialized thickened region of the inner circular smooth muscle layer at the distal esophagus.

questions.q: Inadequate resting tone of the lower esophageal sphincter results in:
questions.explain: Low LES resting tone causes GERD, while failure of LES relaxation causes dysphagia.

items.excerpt: A specialized thickened region of the inner circular layer of smooth muscle at the distal esophagus forms the LES

items.why: Right crus surrounds esophagus; external sphincter

questions.q: The esophagus passes mainly through which diaphragmatic structure, whose contraction augments LES pressure?
questions.explain: The esophagus passes predominantly through the right crus; crural contraction acts as an "external sphincter" in the antireflux barrier.

items.excerpt: Contraction of the crural diaphragm augments lower esophageal sphincter (LES) pressure, functioning as an "external sphincter"

items.why: Esophagus passes through it, ringed by the crura
items.excerpt: The diaphragmatic crura surround the esophagus as it passes through the esophageal hiatus

items.why: End of esophagus; cardia adjacent

questions.q: Which region of the stomach is adjacent to the gastroesophageal junction and receives the swallowed bolus?
questions.explain: The cardia sits next to the GEJ and the LES opening; it receives the bolus and has limited digestive function.

items.excerpt: It begins at the level of C6 and ends at the gastroesophageal junction (GEJ).

items.why: Fundus/cardia/body/antrum/pylorus; regional secretions

questions.q: Which stomach region lies superior to the GEJ and often appears as a gas bubble on imaging?
questions.explain: The fundus is the most superior part of the stomach, above the GEJ, and is often visible as a gas bubble.

questions.q: Gastrin and somatostatin are produced by cells in which region of the stomach?
questions.explain: Cells in the antrum produce gastrin and somatostatin; cells in the body and fundus produce HCl, intrinsic factor, and pepsinogen.

questions.q: HCl, intrinsic factor, and pepsinogen are produced in which gastric regions?
questions.explain: Cells in the body and fundus produce HCl, intrinsic factor, and pepsinogen.

items.excerpt: The stomach consists of five regions: fundus, cardia, body, antrum, and pylorus

items.why: Fundus-formed flap valve; blunted in hiatal hernia

questions.q: When a hiatal hernia displaces the fundus, the angle of His becomes:
choices: Unchanged, with only LES tone falling
questions.explain: The fundus helps form the angle of His, a flap valve; displacing it (hiatal hernia) blunts the angle and predisposes to GERD.

items.excerpt: The fundus of the stomach helps form the esophagogastric angle (angle of His) … creating a flap-valve mechanism that prevents reflux.

items.why: Duodenum 4 parts; jejunum vs ileum; B12 in ileum

questions.q: Which part of the duodenum receives bile and pancreatic secretions via the major duodenal papilla?
questions.explain: The descending (second) part receives bile and pancreatic juice via the major duodenal papilla.

questions.q: Vitamin B12 and bile salts are absorbed mainly in the:
questions.explain: The ileum absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts; the jejunum is particularly important for folate absorption.

questions.q: Compared with the ileum, the jejunum has:
questions.explain: The jejunum has a larger diameter, thicker wall, longer vasa recta, and fewer arcades; the ileum has more fat, shorter vasa recta, and more arcades.

items.excerpt: The jejunum is particularly important for folate absorption, while the ileum absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts.

items.why: D2 receives bile and pancreatic secretions
items.excerpt: Second part (descending): Receives bile and pancreatic secretions via the major duodenal papilla

items.why: Three longitudinal bands; merge at rectosigmoid

questions.q: How many teniae coli are on the colon?
questions.explain: The teniae coli are three longitudinal bands of smooth muscle that aid colonic motility.

questions.q: At the rectosigmoid junction, the teniae coli:
choices: Converge into the internal anal sphincter
Spread to form a continuous muscle layer
Fold inward to form semilunar folds
questions.explain: At the rectosigmoid junction the three teniae spread out and fuse into a continuous outer longitudinal muscle layer around the rectum.

items.excerpt: Teniae coli: three longitudinal bands of smooth muscle that facilitate motility

items.why: Pouch-like sacculations

questions.q: Haustra are best described as:
choices: Fatty tags on the colon surface
questions.explain: Haustra are pouch-like sacculations along the colon, with semilunar folds between them internally.

items.excerpt: Haustra: pouch-like sacculations along the colon

items.why: Small fatty projections

questions.q: Omental appendices are:
choices: Small fatty projections on the colon
questions.explain: Omental appendices are small fatty projections that help distinguish the large intestine from the small intestine.

items.excerpt: Omental appendices: small fatty projections

items.why: Hepatic (right) and splenic (left) flexures

questions.q: The left colic flexure is also called the:
questions.explain: The right colic flexure is the hepatic flexure and the left colic flexure is the splenic flexure.

items.excerpt: Right (hepatic) and left (splenic) colic flexures

items.why: Colon, rectum, anal canal; rectum retroperitoneal

questions.q: Which part of the large intestine is retroperitoneal?
questions.explain: The rectum is a retroperitoneal organ (the R in SAID PUCKER), as are the ascending and descending colon.

items.excerpt: The large intestine extends from the ileocecal valve to the anus and consists of the colon, rectum, and anal canal.

items.why: Five parts; ascending/descending secondarily retroperitoneal

questions.q: Which colon segments are secondarily retroperitoneal?
questions.explain: The ascending and descending colon develop with a mesentery and then fuse to the posterior wall, becoming secondarily retroperitoneal.

questions.q: Which colon segment is S-shaped and stores feces before defecation?
questions.explain: The sigmoid colon stores fecal material before defecation and transitions to the rectum at the rectosigmoid junction.

items.excerpt: The ascending colon is located in the right abdomen and is the primary site for absorption of remaining water and electrolytes.

items.why: Hangs from inferior cecum; mesoappendix

questions.q: The appendix is suspended from the:
questions.explain: The appendix is a narrow tube suspended from the inferior aspect of the cecum by the mesoappendix.

items.excerpt: It is associated with the appendix, a narrow tubular structure suspended from the inferior aspect of the cecum.

items.why: Involuntary relaxation in defecation

questions.q: Which sphincter relaxes involuntarily (autonomic control) during defecation?
questions.explain: Defecation involves involuntary relaxation of the internal anal sphincter and voluntary relaxation of the external anal sphincter.

items.excerpt: Defecation is a coordinated process involving involuntary (autonomic control) relaxation of the internal anal sphincter

items.why: Voluntary (somatic) control

questions.q: Relaxation of the external anal sphincter during defecation is under:
questions.explain: The external anal sphincter is under voluntary (somatic) control, unlike the autonomic internal sphincter.

items.excerpt: voluntary (somatic control) relaxation of the external anal sphincter, allowing controlled passage of stool

items.why: Divides autonomic upper 2/3 from somatic lower 1/3 of anal canal

questions.q: The dentate (pectinate) line separates which parts of the anal canal?
choices: Internal sphincter from the levator ani
questions.explain: The proximal two-thirds of the anal canal is under autonomic control and the distal third under somatic control, divided by the dentate line.

items.excerpt: Its proximal two-thirds is under autonomic control, while the distal third is under somatic control, separated by the dentate (aka pectinate) line.

items.why: End of anal canal
items.excerpt: The anal canal extends from the anorectal junction to the anus.

bricks.title: Anatomy of the Liver, Biliary System, and Exocrine Pancreas

items.why: Right/left/caudate/quadrate; functional lobes

questions.q: Which liver lobe is the only one with direct venous drainage into the IVC?
questions.explain: The caudate lobe, adjacent to the IVC, gets supply from both right and left systems and is the only lobe that drains directly into the IVC.

questions.q: Although it looks like part of the right lobe, the quadrate lobe functionally belongs to the:
questions.explain: The quadrate lobe lies right of the falciform ligament but receives blood supply and biliary drainage with the functional left lobe.

items.excerpt: Importantly, the caudate lobe is the only lobe with direct venous drainage into the IVC.

items.why: Hilum between caudate and quadrate; PV, PHA, CHD

questions.q: Which structure does NOT pass through the porta hepatis?
questions.explain: The porta hepatis transmits the portal vein, proper hepatic artery, common hepatic duct, lymphatics, and nerves; the IVC is embedded beside the caudate lobe.

questions.q: The porta hepatis lies on the visceral surface between which two lobes?
questions.explain: The porta hepatis, the hilum of the liver, lies between the caudate and quadrate lobes on the visceral surface.

items.excerpt: Located on the visceral surface of the liver between the caudate and quadrate lobes, the porta hepatis transmits the hepatic portal vein … common hepatic duct

items.why: Separates anatomical right and left lobes

questions.q: Which structure divides the anatomical right and left lobes of the liver?
questions.explain: The right and left anatomical lobes are divided by the falciform ligament, which attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall.

items.excerpt: The right and left lobes are divided by the falciform ligament.

items.why: In falciform ligament; umbilical vein remnant

questions.q: The ligamentum teres lies within which ligament?
questions.explain: The falciform ligament contains the ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver), the remnant of the fetal umbilical vein.

items.excerpt: The falciform ligament contains the ligamentum teres which is a remnant of the fetal umbilical vein (otherwise known as the round ligament of the liver).

items.why: Peritoneal reflection from liver to diaphragm
items.excerpt: The coronary and triangular ligaments are reflections of peritoneum coursing from the diaphragmatic surface of the liver to the diaphragm.

items.why: Contains right and left gastric vessels

questions.q: The hepatogastric ligament carries which vessels?
questions.explain: The hepatogastric ligament (liver to stomach) contains the left and right gastric vessels; the portal triad runs in the hepatoduodenal ligament.

items.excerpt: the hepatogastric ligament, which connects the liver to the stomach and contains the left and right gastric vessels

items.why: Portal triad; Pringle maneuver

questions.q: A surgeon controls severe liver bleeding with the Pringle maneuver. Which structure is clamped?
questions.explain: The Pringle maneuver occludes the hepatoduodenal ligament, stopping inflow through the portal vein and hepatic artery.

items.excerpt: The Pringle maneuver, hepatic inflow occlusion, temporarily occludes the hepatoduodenal ligament, halting hepatic inflow through the portal vein and hepatic artery

items.why: Gives left gastric, splenic, common hepatic
items.excerpt: The celiac trunk has three branches … Left gastric artery … Splenic artery … Common hepatic artery

items.why: Celiac branch; becomes proper hepatic

questions.q: Besides the proper hepatic artery, the common hepatic artery gives rise to the:
questions.explain: The common hepatic artery branches into the proper hepatic artery and the gastroduodenal artery.

items.excerpt: The common hepatic artery enters the hepatoduodenal ligament of the liver. It then gives rise to the proper hepatic artery.

items.why: Oxygenated inflow; divides into R/L hepatic

questions.q: The proper hepatic artery divides into the:
questions.explain: The proper hepatic artery brings oxygenated blood to the liver and divides into right and left hepatic arteries for each side.

items.excerpt: The proper hepatic artery, which brings oxygenated blood to the liver

items.why: Supply functional lobes; right hepatic gives cystic

questions.q: The cystic artery is most commonly a branch of the:
questions.explain: The cystic artery most commonly arises from the right hepatic artery and is found in Calot's triangle.

items.excerpt: Eventually, the proper hepatic artery divides into the left and right hepatic arteries, which supply the left and right sides of the liver, respectively.

items.why: SMV + splenic; nutrient-rich inflow

questions.q: The hepatic portal vein is formed by the joining of the:
questions.explain: The portal vein forms from the superior mesenteric and splenic veins; the IMV joins via the splenic vein.

items.excerpt: The portal vein carries nutrient-rich blood from the gastrointestinal tract, spleen, pancreas, and gallbladder to the liver for processing, storage, metabolism, and detoxification.

items.why: Joins splenic v. to form portal v.
items.excerpt: The hepatic portal vein is formed from the joining of the superior mesenteric vein and the splenic vein.

items.why: Joins portal circulation via splenic v.
items.excerpt: The inferior mesenteric vein also joins the portal circulation via the splenic vein.

items.why: Middle hepatic v. divides functional lobes

questions.q: The functional right and left lobes of the liver are separated by the:
questions.explain: Functional lobes are defined by vascular inflow and biliary drainage and are separated by the middle hepatic vein, not the falciform ligament.

items.excerpt: The functional right and left lobes are separated by the middle hepatic vein

items.why: Drain liver directly into IVC
items.excerpt: the right, middle, and left hepatic veins drain directly into the inferior vena cava

items.why: Receives hepatic veins + caudate drainage

questions.q: The right, middle, and left hepatic veins drain into which vessel just beneath the diaphragm?
questions.explain: Sinusoids drain to central veins and then to the hepatic veins, which empty directly into the IVC at the superior liver.

items.excerpt: A section of the inferior vena cava is embedded in the liver to the right of the caudate lobe.

items.why: Parasympathetics to liver and pancreas

questions.q: Preganglionic vagal fibers to the pancreas pass through the celiac ganglion and then:
choices: Synapse in ganglia within the pancreas
Synapse in the superior mesenteric ganglion
questions.explain: Posterior vagal trunk fibers pass through the celiac ganglion without synapsing and synapse in ganglia within the pancreas.

questions.q: Vagal acetylcholine release at the pancreas stimulates:
questions.explain: Vagal ACh stimulates digestive juice release from acinar cells and insulin release from β cells ("rest and digest").

items.excerpt: parasympathetic innervation from the vagal trunks is involved in modulating bile secretion and hepatic metabolic activity

items.why: Join to form common hepatic duct

questions.q: The right and left hepatic ducts join to form the:
questions.explain: Bile canaliculi merge into bile ducts, then the right and left hepatic ducts, which join to form the common hepatic duct.

items.excerpt: The right and left hepatic ducts join to form the common hepatic duct

items.why: Exits porta hepatis; + cystic -> CBD; Calot border

questions.q: The common hepatic duct joins which duct to form the common bile duct?
questions.explain: The common hepatic duct leaves the porta hepatis and joins the cystic duct to form the common bile duct.

items.excerpt: The common hepatic duct exits the liver at the porta hepatis and then joins the cystic duct … to form the common bile duct

items.why: CHD + cystic; to ampulla; stone -> jaundice

questions.q: A gallstone impacted in the common bile duct (choledocholithiasis) typically causes:
questions.explain: Choledocholithiasis impairs bile drainage from the liver and can cause jaundice.

questions.q: Cancer of the pancreatic head causes jaundice mainly by compressing the:
questions.explain: The common bile duct passes behind/through the pancreatic head, so a head mass can obstruct it and cause jaundice.

items.excerpt: A gallstone may also pass through the cystic duct and enter the common bile duct. If it becomes lodged there, the condition is called choledocholithiasis

items.why: CBD + pancreatic duct; stone -> gallstone pancreatitis

questions.q: A gallstone impacted at the ampulla of Vater can obstruct both ducts and cause:
questions.explain: Impaction at the ampulla blocks both the common bile duct and pancreatic duct and can cause gallstone pancreatitis.

items.excerpt: If a gallstone becomes impacted at the ampulla of Vater, it may obstruct both the common bile duct and pancreatic duct

items.why: Medial wall D2; sphincter of Oddi

questions.q: The major duodenal papilla is located on the:
choices: Lateral wall of the second part
Posterior wall of the third part
Medial wall of the second part
Anterior wall of the first part
questions.explain: The ampulla and sphincter of Oddi form the major duodenal papilla on the medial wall of the second (descending) duodenum.

questions.q: Which structure controls the flow of bile and pancreatic juice through the major duodenal papilla?
questions.explain: The sphincter of Oddi is a muscular ring around the ampulla that controls the flow of bile and pancreatic secretions into the duodenum.

items.excerpt: Together, the ampulla and sphincter form the major duodenal papilla on the medial wall of the second portion of the duodenum.

items.why: Stores bile; fundus/body/neck; shoulder-referred pain

questions.q: Which part of the gallbladder is continuous with the cystic duct?
questions.explain: The gallbladder has a fundus, body, and neck; the neck continues as the cystic duct.

questions.q: Gallbladder inflammation irritating the overlying peritoneum and diaphragm may refer sharp pain to the:
questions.explain: Somatic pain from the peritoneum over the liver and gallbladder travels in the phrenic nerve (C3–C5), so it is referred to the right shoulder.

items.excerpt: Its main function is to store bile made in the liver and release it in a pulse when needed in the duodenum

items.why: From gallbladder neck; stone -> cholecystitis

questions.q: A gallstone lodged in the cystic duct most typically causes:
questions.explain: A stone in the gallbladder neck or cystic duct blocks bile outflow from the gallbladder, causing acute cholecystitis.

items.excerpt: If a gallstone becomes lodged in the gallbladder neck or cystic duct, obstruction of bile outflow can lead to acute cholecystitis

items.why: Usually from right hepatic; in Calot's triangle

questions.q: During cholecystectomy, the cystic artery is found in Calot's triangle. What are its borders?
questions.explain: Calot's (hepatobiliary) triangle is bounded by the liver edge, the common hepatic duct, and the cystic duct.

items.excerpt: The cystic artery is most commonly a branch of the right hepatic artery.

items.why: Head/neck/body/tail relations; retroperitoneal; pain to mid-back

questions.q: The uncinate process of the pancreatic head lies posterior to the:
questions.explain: The uncinate process is the part of the pancreatic head posterior to the superior mesenteric artery and vein.

questions.q: The tail of the pancreas lies anterior to the left kidney and extends toward the:
questions.explain: The pancreatic tail lies anterior to the left kidney and extends toward the splenic hilum.

questions.q: Besides the epigastrium, pancreatic pain is often referred to the:
questions.explain: Pancreatic afferents reach T6–T9, which also receive input from the epigastrium and mid back, so pain is felt in both.

items.excerpt: The head lies in the curve of the duodenum, anterior to the inferior vena cava and the common bile duct.

items.why: Runs length of pancreas; joins CBD at ampulla

questions.q: The main pancreatic duct joins which duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla?
questions.explain: The main pancreatic duct runs along the length of the pancreas and joins the common bile duct at the ampulla of Vater.

items.excerpt: The main pancreatic duct carries the digestive enzymes produced in the pancreas to the duodenum.

items.why: Duodenum curves around pancreatic head
items.excerpt: The pancreas and duodenum lie at the junction of the foregut and midgut, with the transition occurring near the major duodenal papilla.

items.why: CHA branch; gives superior pancreaticoduodenals

questions.q: The anterior and posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries arise from the:
questions.explain: The gastroduodenal artery (from the common hepatic) divides into the anterior and posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries.

items.excerpt: The gastroduodenal artery divides into the anterior and posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries.

items.why: Duodenum + pancreatic head; anastomose with inferior

questions.q: The superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries anastomose with the inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries, a branch of the:
questions.explain: The pancreatic head sits at the foregut–midgut junction, so celiac (superior) and SMA (inferior) pancreaticoduodenal arteries anastomose there.

items.excerpt: The anterior and posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries supply the duodenum and head of the pancreas.

items.why: Superior border of pancreas; body and tail

questions.q: Which part of the pancreas does the splenic artery supply as it runs along the pancreas's superior border?
questions.explain: The splenic artery courses along the superior border of the pancreas, directly supplying the body and tail before reaching the spleen.

items.excerpt: The splenic artery courses along the superior border of the pancreas, directly supplying its body and tail before reaching the spleen

items.why: LUQ under ribs 9-11; splenomegaly rupture risk

questions.q: The spleen lies in the left upper quadrant beneath which ribs?
questions.explain: The spleen lies in the left upper quadrant beneath ribs 9–11, receiving the splenic artery at its hilum.

questions.q: A patient with infectious mononucleosis has splenomegaly. After a minor blow to the abdomen, which complication is most feared?
questions.explain: An enlarged spleen extends below the costal margin and is more fragile, so even minor trauma can cause rupture and life-threatening hemorrhage.

items.excerpt: The enlarged spleen … is more fragile than the normal spleen, increasing the risk of rupture even with minor trauma.

items.why: Behind pancreatic neck, in front of D3

questions.q: Together with the SMV, the superior mesenteric artery passes:
choices: In front of the pancreatic neck, behind D3
Behind the pancreatic tail, in front of D2
Behind the pancreatic neck, in front of D3
Behind the stomach, in front of the left kidney
questions.explain: The SMA and SMV pass posterior to the neck of the pancreas and anterior to the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum.

items.excerpt: with the superior mesenteric vein (SMV), it passes posterior to the neck of the pancreas and anterior to the third (transverse) portion of the duodenum.

items.why: First branch of SMA; inferior head

questions.q: The inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery supplies which part of the pancreas?
questions.explain: The inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery, the first branch of the SMA, splits into anterior and posterior rami serving the inferior pancreatic head.

items.excerpt: The inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery is the first branch of the SMA.

items.why: Drains pancreatic body/tail to portal v.

questions.q: Venous blood from the body and tail of the pancreas drains mainly into the:
questions.explain: Pancreatic venous drainage is predominantly via the splenic vein, which carries blood from the body and tail to the portal vein.

items.excerpt: The splenic vein collects blood from the body and tail of the pancreas, delivering it to the hepatic portal vein.

items.why: Parasympathetic: stimulates pancreatic secretion
items.excerpt: When the vagus nerve releases acetylcholine, it stimulates release of digestive juices from acinar cells and insulin from β cells.

items.why: Vagal fibers pass through without synapsing
items.excerpt: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the posterior vagal trunk first pass through the celiac ganglion without synapsing and then travel to ganglia within the pancreas.

items.why: Sympathetic to pancreas; afferents T6-T9

questions.q: Sympathetic stimulation via the splanchnic nerves increases which pancreatic secretion?
questions.explain: Sympathetic input mostly inhibits pancreatic secretion; the exception is increased glucagon release from α cells.

questions.q: Pancreatic visceral pain afferents travel with the splanchnic nerves to which spinal levels?
questions.explain: Pancreatic afferents pass through the celiac ganglia and travel with sympathetic splanchnic nerves to dorsal root ganglia at T6–T9.

items.excerpt: The visceral afferent fibers travel with sympathetic splanchnic nerves to the dorsal root ganglia at T6–T9.

bricks.title: Anatomy of the Femoral and Inguinal Regions

items.why: Midline sternum->pelvis; vertical fibers; spine flexion

questions.q: Which way do the fibers of the rectus abdominis run?
questions.explain: The paired rectus abdominis run vertically in the midline from the sternum to the pelvis, flexing the spine and raising abdominal pressure.

items.excerpt: They run midline, connecting the sternum to the pelvis. They are key in generating abdominal pressure and flexing the spine.

items.why: Midline 'zipper'; diastasis recti; midline laparotomy

questions.q: A postpartum patient has a midline bulge when raising her head from supine, with no fascial defect. Which structure is most involved?
questions.explain: Diastasis recti is widening and thinning of the linea alba, not a true fascial defect, so there is no incarceration risk.

questions.q: A midline laparotomy enters the abdomen by:
questions.explain: A midline laparotomy divides no muscle; it passes through the linea alba between the right and left rectus abdominis.

items.excerpt: Diastasis recti presents as a midline abdominal bulge … due to widening and attenuation of the linea alba rather than a true fascial defect

items.why: Largest, most superficial; inferomedial fibers

questions.q: A patient strains and injures the most superficial lateral abdominal muscle. Which way do its fibers run?
questions.explain: The external oblique is the largest and most superficial lateral muscle, with fibers running inferomedially ("hands in pockets").

items.excerpt: External oblique: This muscle is the largest and most superficial of the three, with its fibers running in an inferomedial direction

items.why: Fibers 90 deg to EO; splits above arcuate line

questions.q: The fibers of the internal oblique run:
questions.explain: The internal oblique lies deep to the external oblique, with fibers running at 90° to it.

items.excerpt: Above the arcuate line, the internal oblique aponeurosis splits to contribute to both the anterior and posterior rectus sheaths.

items.why: Deepest; horizontal fibers

questions.q: Which lateral abdominal wall muscle is the deepest, with horizontal fibers?
questions.explain: Transversus abdominis is the deepest of the three lateral muscles, with horizontal fibers.

items.excerpt: Transversus (transverse) abdominis: This muscle is the deepest, with horizontal fibers.

items.why: Fatty superficial fascia

questions.q: Camper fascia is the:
questions.explain: Superficial to the muscles (deep to superficial) are the membranous (Scarpa) fascia, fat (Camper fascia), and skin.

items.excerpt: It would go through, in order, the following: skin, subcutaneous fat (Camper fascia), membranous fascia (Scarpa fascia)

items.why: Membranous layer deep to Camper

questions.q: In an open appendectomy incision, which layer is cut immediately after Camper fascia?
questions.explain: The RLQ incision passes skin, Camper fascia, Scarpa fascia, external oblique, internal oblique, transversus, transversalis fascia, preperitoneal fat, and peritoneum.

items.excerpt: Superficial to these muscles (listing from deep to superficial) are the membranous (Scarpa) fascia, fat (Camper fascia), and skin.

items.why: Aponeuroses; arcuate line transition

questions.q: Below the arcuate line, how are the lateral muscle aponeuroses arranged?
choices: Internal oblique splits around the rectus
All pass posterior to the rectus
All pass anterior to the rectus
questions.explain: Below the arcuate line all three aponeuroses pass anterior to the rectus abdominis, leaving no posterior rectus sheath.

items.excerpt: The arcuate line is the transition from both an anterior and posterior rectus sheath to only an anterior rectus sheath.

items.why: L1 contribution to abdominal wall

questions.q: The iliohypogastric nerve adds sensory and motor supply to the abdominal wall from which spinal level?
questions.explain: The anterior wall is supplied by T7–T12 plus L1 via the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves, giving T7–L1 dermatomes.

items.excerpt: with additional motor and sensory contributions from L1 via the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves

items.why: Internal thoracic branch; anastomosis in rectus sheath

questions.q: The superior epigastric artery is a terminal branch of the:
questions.explain: The superior epigastric (from the internal thoracic) and inferior epigastric (from the external iliac) arteries anastomose within the rectus sheath.

items.excerpt: The superior epigastric artery, a terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery, and the inferior epigastric artery … form an important anastomosis within the rectus sheath

items.why: External iliac branch; Hesselbach lateral border; hematoma

questions.q: The inferior epigastric artery arises from the:
questions.explain: The inferior epigastric artery is a branch of the external iliac artery and enters the rectus sheath near the arcuate line.

questions.q: Why does inferior epigastric bleeding produce larger rectus sheath hematomas than superior epigastric bleeding?
choices: It is a larger artery than the superior
No posterior sheath below arcuate line
It runs within the linea alba
questions.explain: Below the arcuate line the posterior rectus sheath is absent, so inferior epigastric bleeding is less confined.

items.excerpt: Because the posterior rectus sheath is absent below the arcuate line, bleeding from the inferior epigastric artery is less confined and may produce larger hematomas

items.why: Inguinal lig / sartorius / adductor longus; femoral vessels

questions.q: What forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle?
questions.explain: The femoral triangle is bounded by the inguinal ligament (superior), sartorius (lateral), and adductor longus (medial).

questions.q: To draw blood from the femoral vein in the femoral triangle, where should the needle go?
questions.explain: The femoral vein lies medial to the femoral artery; palpate the arterial pulse and insert the needle just medial to it.

items.excerpt: The femoral triangle is bordered by the inguinal ligament, sartorius muscle, and adductor longus muscle

items.why: Lateral attachment of inguinal ligament

questions.q: The inguinal ligament spans from the anterior superior iliac spine to the:
questions.explain: The inguinal ligament, the superior border of the femoral triangle, spans from the ASIS to the pubic bone.

items.excerpt: Superior border: Inguinal Ligament … spans from the anterior superior iliac spine to pubic bone

items.why: Wraps artery, vein, lymphatics (not nerve)

questions.q: Within the femoral sheath, the femoral vein occupies which compartment?
questions.explain: The femoral artery is in the lateral compartment, the vein in the intermediate, and the femoral canal in the medial compartment.

items.excerpt: The femoral artery, vein, and lymphatics reside within a fibrous wrapping called the femoral sheath

items.why: Medial compartment; femoral hernias

questions.q: During femoral hernia repair, which structure lies just superior to the herniated bowel?
questions.explain: Femoral hernias pass through the femoral canal just below the inguinal ligament and medial to the femoral vein.

questions.q: Females are more likely than males to develop femoral hernias because of a:
questions.explain: Females have a wider pelvis and femoral canal, so they get femoral hernias more often than males, though inguinal hernias are still more common in both.

items.excerpt: The femoral canal, just below the inguinal ligament and medial to the femoral vein, is where femoral hernias occur.

items.why: Lateral, outside femoral sheath; NAVEL

questions.q: From lateral to medial, which order describes the structures passing under the inguinal ligament?
questions.explain: NAVEL, lateral to medial: femoral Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space (femoral canal) with Lymphatics.

questions.q: A stab wound damages the femoral sheath but spares structures outside it. Which is least likely injured?
questions.explain: The femoral artery, vein, and lymphatics lie inside the femoral sheath; the femoral nerve runs outside it, just lateral.

items.excerpt: The femoral nerve runs outside the femoral sheath just laterally.

items.why: Deep ring (lateral to IEV) -> superficial ring; indirect hernia

questions.q: Relative to the inferior epigastric vessels, the deep inguinal ring lies:
questions.explain: The deep ring is an opening in the transversalis fascia just lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; indirect hernias enter here.

questions.q: A 5-month-old boy has a groin mass from abdominal contents passing through the deep ring into the inguinal canal. Diagnosis?
questions.explain: Indirect hernias pass obliquely through the deep inguinal ring and inguinal canal and are most common in males, especially infants.

items.excerpt: the passageway starts at an opening in the transversalis fascia just lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; this opening is called the deep inguinal ring

items.why: Superficial ring; anterior wall of canal

questions.q: The superficial inguinal ring is an opening in the:
questions.explain: The four canal walls converge at the superficial inguinal ring, an opening in the external oblique aponeurosis; that aponeurosis also forms most of the anterior wall.

items.excerpt: The anterior wall is derived predominately from the external oblique aponeurosis with some contribution from the internal oblique aponeurosis.

items.why: Superficial ring lies above it

questions.q: The superficial inguinal ring lies directly above the:
questions.explain: The superficial inguinal ring lies directly above the pubic crest.

items.excerpt: The superficial inguinal ring lies directly above the pubic crest.

items.why: Male canal content; processus vaginalis -> indirect hernia

questions.q: Indirect inguinal hernias are much more common in males mainly because of:
questions.explain: Indirect hernias are more frequent in males due to persistence of the processus vaginalis and passage of the spermatic cord through the canal.

items.excerpt: they occur much more frequently in males due to persistence of the processus vaginalis … and passage of the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal

items.why: Female canal content, to mons pubis

questions.q: In females, the round ligament of the uterus passes through the inguinal canal to the:
questions.explain: In females the inguinal canal contains the round ligament of the uterus, which passes to the mons pubis.

items.excerpt: In females, the inguinal canal contains the round ligament of the uterus to the mons pubis.

items.why: L1; in inguinal canal (both sexes)

questions.q: Which nerve travels within the inguinal canal in both males and females?
questions.explain: Both the female and male inguinal canals contain the ilioinguinal nerve, the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, vessels, and lymphatics.

items.excerpt: Both the female and male inguinal canals contain the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, ilioinguinal nerve, blood vessels, and lymphatics.

items.why: Rectus abdominis / IEV / inguinal ligament; direct hernia

questions.q: What are the borders of the inguinal (Hesselbach) triangle?
choices: Rectus abdominis, femoral vein, lacunar ligament
Inferior epigastrics, sartorius, pubic crest line
Rectus abdominis, inferior epigastrics, inguinal ligament
questions.explain: Hesselbach's triangle is bounded by the rectus abdominis (medial), inferior epigastric vessels (lateral), and inguinal ligament (inferior).

questions.q: A hernia that protrudes straight through the inguinal triangle due to abdominal wall weakness is a:
questions.explain: Herniation through the inguinal triangle (medial to the inferior epigastric vessels) is a direct inguinal hernia.

items.excerpt: The inguinal (Hesselbach) triangle is bordered by the rectus abdominis medially, the inferior epigastric vessels laterally, and the inguinal ligament inferiorly

items.why: Deep to TA; deep ring; posterior wall of canal

questions.q: The posterior wall of the inguinal canal is formed mainly by the:
questions.explain: The posterior wall of the inguinal canal and the floor of the inguinal triangle are formed primarily by the transversalis fascia.

questions.q: The deep inguinal ring is an opening in which layer?
questions.explain: The deep inguinal ring is an opening in the transversalis fascia just lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

items.excerpt: The floor/posterior wall of the inguinal triangle is formed primarily by the transversalis fascia, with no muscular contribution from transversus abdominis.
